verses.text: For Yahweh will have compassion on Jacob, and will yet choose Israel, and set them in their own land. The foreigner will join himself with them, and they will unite with the house of Jacob.

The peoples will take them, and bring them to their place. The house of Israel will possess them in Yahweh’s land for servants and for handmaids. They will take as captives those whose captives they were; and they shall rule over their oppressors.
It will happen in the day that Yahweh will give you rest from your sorrow, from your trouble, and from the hard service in which you were made to serve,
that you will take up this parable against the king of Babylon, and say, “How the oppressor has ceased! The golden city has ceased!”
Yahweh has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of the rulers,
who struck the peoples in wrath with a continual stroke, who ruled the nations in anger, with a persecution that no one restrained.
The whole earth is at rest, and is quiet. They break out song.
Yes, the cypress trees rejoice with you, with the cedars of Lebanon, saying, “Since you are humbled, no lumberjack has come up against us.”

Sheol  from beneath has moved for you to meet you at your coming. It stirs up the departed spirits for you, even all the rulers of the earth. It has raised up from their thrones all the kings of the nations.
They all will answer and ask you, “Have you also become as weak as we are? Have you become like us?”
Your pomp is brought down to Sheol,  with the sound of your stringed instruments. Maggots are spread out under you, and worms cover you.
How you have fallen from heaven, morning star, son of the dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, who laid the nations low!
You said in your heart, “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north!
I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!”
Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol,  to the depths of the pit.
Those who see you will stare at you. They will ponder you, saying, “Is this the man who made the earth to tremble, who shook kingdoms;
who made the world like a wilderness, and overthrew its cities; who didn’t release his prisoners to their home?”
All the kings of the nations, sleep in glory, everyone in his own house.

But you are cast away from your tomb like an abominable branch, clothed with the slain, who are thrust through with the sword, who go down to the stones of the pit; like a dead body trodden under foot.
You will not join them in burial, because you have destroyed your land. You have killed your people. The offspring  of evildoers will not be named forever.
Prepare for slaughter of his children because of the iniquity of their fathers, that they not rise up and possess the earth, and fill the surface of the world with cities.
“I will rise up against them,” says Yahweh of Armies, “and cut off from Babylon name and remnant, and son and son’s son,” says Yahweh.
“I will also make it a possession for the porcupine, and pools of water. I will sweep it with the broom of destruction,” says Yahweh of Armies.
Yahweh of Armies has sworn, saying, “Surely, as I have thought, so shall it happen; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand:
that I will break the Assyrian in my land, and tread him under foot on my mountains. Then his yoke will leave them, and his burden leave their shoulders.
This is the plan that is determined for the whole earth. This is the hand that is stretched out over all the nations.
For Yahweh of Armies has planned, and who can stop it? His hand is stretched out, and who can turn it back?”
This burden was in the year that king Ahaz died.
Don’t rejoice, O Philistia, all of you, because the rod that struck you is broken; for out of the serpent’s root an adder will emerge, and his fruit will be a fiery flying serpent.
The firstborn of the poor will eat, and the needy will lie down in safety; and I will kill your root with famine, and your remnant will be killed.
Howl, gate! Cry, city! You are melted away, Philistia, all of you; for smoke comes out of the north, and there is no straggler in his ranks.
What will they answer the messengers of the nation? That Yahweh has founded Zion, and in her the afflicted of his people will take refuge.

footnotes.content: The Lord says 'I will have compassion'—not 'you must earn it.' That's where all freedom begins. Notice how foreigners join Israel not through conquest but through mercy; the same Lord who breaks chains invites wanderers in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A startling reversal: the captives become the masters, the oppressed inherit what was stolen. The Lord does not forget the humble; He turns their sorrow into an inheritance. This is how Jesus calls us—from servants to sons.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rest from sorrow. Rest from trouble. Rest from hard service. The promise isn't ease—it's that God Himself will lay down the burden you've carried too long. In Him, we finally stop struggling alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A parable—a wisdom song—rises against the tyrant of Babylon. The 'golden city has ceased.' Even the most glittering power falls when it trusts itself instead of God. The oppressor's end is written before his cruelty begins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The staff of the wicked—the rod of command, the tool of violence—is broken by the Lord's hand. No dictator's scepter outlasts Him. He alone holds true authority, and He breaks what crushes the weak.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'With a continual stroke'—relentless cruelty. But notice: there was one who 'restrained' nothing, one who endured all the nations' rage so we would not have to. The ruler's worst anger is nothing to what Jesus bore for us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rest. Quiet. A whole earth at peace for once. When the hand that choked the world is stayed, even creation itself exhales. This is what we long for—the kingdom where no one rules with iron anymore.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cedar trees of Lebanon—symbols of Lebanon's wealth—rejoice. Lumberjacks came no more to fell them. Nature itself celebrates when tyranny ends and the strong are at last humbled. Even the trees know when justice comes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sheol stirs. The dead look up—a picture of how far pride falls. Kings who ruled earth are leveled to one kingdom beneath. Death makes all thrones equal. Only one throne—Christ's—stands above death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Have you become like us?' Death asks the tyrant the same question it asks every soul: Did your power shield you? No. In the grave, the mighty and the meek lie down together. That levels everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pomp brought down. Stringed instruments silent. Maggots and worms—a grim reminder that all grandeur is dust. Yet believers in Jesus know: He alone will raise us incorruptible, clothed in glory, not shame.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Morning star'—how bright he was. How far he fell. This speaks to the mystery of pride: the more brilliant the light, the darker the shadow when it turns to self-worship. Jesus alone deserves such worship, and He willingly stoops.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five 'I wills'—the litany of self-exaltation. 'I will ascend... I will exalt... I will sit...' This is the root sin: the refusal to bow, the insistence on the throne. All human rebellion echoes this same proud word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'I will make myself like the Most High.' To sit on His throne, to wear His crown—that's the deepest temptation, whispered to Adam and Eve, to Babylon, to every human heart. Jesus alone is Most High, and His humility proves His power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But—one word that crushes all ambition. Down to Sheol. Down to the pit. 'But' is the hinge on which kingdoms turn. All our 'I wills' meet God's 'Yet you shall be brought down.' Mercy is the only escape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Staring. Pondering. The mighty reduced to a riddle, a corpse picked over by history. What looked invincible in his day seems pathetic in death. This is God's way of teaching: strip all pretense and we see who we truly are.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wilderness. Overthrown cities. Prisoners not released. The bill of all his cruelties is now read aloud. He 'didn't release' others; the Lord will not release him from his deserved judgment. Only Christ's blood releases us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the kings sleep in glory, each in his own house. A custom of burial, a dignity of rest—even kings of nations receive it. But not this one. His shame is part of his judgment, a final dishonoring.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cast away like refuse. Clothed with the slain. Thrust through with the sword. This is degradation—no tomb, no honor, a body trampled in the pit. Yet even this horror pales beside the shame Christ bore willingly for our sake.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No burial. No name. His offspring forgotten. A double death—he dies twice, once in body, once in memory. The Lord teaches: your name lives only in Him. That's why Jesus promises, 'I will write on them the name of my God.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The children bear the father's sin. A hard word—yet it teaches that corruption spreads, that tyranny breeds tyranny. Only the cross breaks the chain. Only Christ's blood cleanses a generation and calls it 'new.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'I will rise up against them,' says the Lord. Not in rage—in justice. The armies of God are not cruel; they are righteous. Name and remnant, sons and grandsons—all absorbed into the dust of history. The Lord is patient, but He is also sovereign.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Babylon becomes the porcupine's home, pools of water. A mighty city, a throne of empire, reduced to wilderness. 'I will sweep it with the broom of destruction'—such plain, final language for the end of human pride.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An oath. 'Surely, as I have thought...' God speaks with the certainty of One who plans and accomplishes. He doesn't hope His purposes will stand; He swears they will. We can rest in that—His word is unshakeable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Assyria—a historical power that threatened Israel—will be broken on God's mountains, trodden under His feet. Its yoke lifts from the shoulders of the people. A specific promise that echoes all God's future deliverances.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The plan determined for the whole earth. His hand stretched over all nations. What comfort in that verse: nothing surprises Him, no empire rises outside His sight. The universe is not chaos—it bends toward His kingdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Who can stop it? Who can turn it back?' The Lord invites us to look at His hand and see: nothing thwarts Him. Not Babylon, not Assyria, not the powers of this age. His counsel stands forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The burden was in the year King Ahaz died—a historical marker. This prophecy was given at a specific moment, to a real people in real peril. God's Word always meets us in time and place, not in abstraction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Don't rejoice, O Philistia.' A warning wrapped in irony: your oppressor is fallen, yes, but a worse evil stirs. The serpent's root brings forth an adder, a flying serpent. One danger passes only if we turn to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The firstborn of the poor will eat. The needy will lie down in safety. But Philistia's root withers by famine, its remnant killed. God's heart is for the humble and suffering. He ensures they shall be fed and safe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Howl, gate! Cry, city! Smoke from the north—invasion, judgment, the walls crumbling. Yet this same prophet speaks to Israel: do not fear. Your God is with you. We, too, live in a world where kingdoms fall, yet we are called to trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this closing word: 'Yahweh has founded Zion.' No matter what empires crumble around us, no matter what news shakes the earth, the Lord has a city, a refuge. In Jesus, we are stones in that city, built on a foundation that will not fail.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
